Operator
Good day. Thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q3 2025 Comstock Resources Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during this session, you need to press star one one on your telephone. You will hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your first speaker today, Jay Allison, Chairman and CEO. Please go ahead.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
All right. Again, I want to thank you for the introduction, and thank those that are on the call. It's been a really good morning. You know, welcome to the Comstock Resources Q3 2025 Financial and Operating Results Conference Call. You can view a slide presentation during or after this call by going to our website at www.comstockresources.com and downloading the quarterly results presentation. There you'll find a presentation entitled Q3 2025 Results. I'm Jay Allison, Chief Executive Officer of Comstock. With me is Roland Burns, our President and CFO, Dan Harrison, our COO, and Ron Mills, our VP of Finance and Investor Relations. Please refer to slide two in our presentations and note that our discussions today will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of securities laws.
While we believe the expectations of such statements to be reasonable, there can be no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct. If you'll flip over to slide three. You know, as we start today, we are really excited to update our stakeholders on the company's progress so far this year. Comstock and our bold move to create the Western extension of the Haynesville Shale have been the subject of several news stories recently, as the interest in natural gas has never been greater. I don't believe we have ever seen a brighter future for natural gas. Natural gas has become the go-to energy source in United States, driven by the growth in LNG exports and the push to generate power for AI and data center development.
I noticed yesterday that LNG exports reached a record high of 18.7 Bcf, and the journal is full of articles on the impact of AI and data centers on future power demand. The Haynesville Shale is on the front line to deliver the gas supply to meet the growing demand. As one of the early pioneers in the Haynesville, we have focused our efforts over the last five years on being a leader in expanding the resource in the basin to be able to meet the new demand. The Western Haynesville story is more about utilizing advancements in technology than geologic prospecting, as the existence of the Haynesville and Bossier Shale in the area has been well known.
Today, we're giving you a preview of the future by providing our estimates of the vast inventory of drilling locations in our emerging play in the Western Haynesville. We also announced the divestiture of some of our Legacy Haynesville assets, which we will not need in the future as we shift more of our resources to the Western Haynesville. The sale allows us to improve our balance sheet as all of the proceeds will retire long-term debt. You know, this was also a very efficient quarter in our Legacy Haynesville drilling program, fueled by the additional drilling rig we added at the beginning of the quarter. Our drilling and completion cost in our Legacy Haynesville area averaged $1,229 per lateral foot. That is an industry-leading number in the basin.
The activity we added last quarter will drive production growth next year into a growing demand market. On slide three, we summarize the highlights of Q3. Higher natural gas prices in Q3 drove the improved financial results in the quarter compared to Q3 of 2024. Our natural gas and oil sales grew to $335 million. We generated $190 million of operating cash flow, or $0.65 per diluted share. Adjusted EBITDAX for the quarter was $249 million, and we reported adjusted net income of $28 million or $0.09 per diluted share. During Q3, we put three new Western Haynesville wells online, increasing the number of wells turned to sales in 2025 in the Western Haynesville to eight wells.
Those three wells had an average lateral length of 8,566 feet and an average per well initial production rate of 32,000,000 cubic feet per day. In our Legacy Haynesville, we've now turned 28 wells to sales to date in 2025, with an average lateral length of 11,919 feet and a per well initial production rate of 25,000,000 cubic feet per day. In September, we divested of our non-strategic Cotton Valley wells in East Texas and North Louisiana for net proceeds of $15.2 million. We also recently entered into agreement to divest of our Shelby Trough assets in East Texas for $430 million in cash, and that sale is expected to close in December. On the next slide, I will cover the divestitures in more detail. Slide four.
Visually, you can see this. It summarizes our recent divestitures. In September, we sold our legacy Cotton Valley wells in East Texas, North Louisiana for net proceeds of $15.2 million. Our Cotton Valley properties, which we sold, included 880 or 770.9 net wells, producing 7.9 million cubic feet per day net to our interest and another 46 for 27.3 net inactive wells. On 10 October, we entered into an agreement to sell our Shelby Trough properties in Nacogdoches, San Augustine, and Sabine counties for $430 million. These assets include 36,000 net acres with 155 or 74.5 net wells, producing 9.300,000 cubic feet per day net to our interest. The Shelby Trough sale is expected to close in December. I'll now turn it over to Roland to discuss financial results we report today. Roland?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
All right. Thanks, Jay. Slide five, we cover our Q3 financial results. Production in Q3 averaged 1.22 Bcfe a day, and our oil and gas sales in the quarter increased 10% from the Q3 of last year to $335 million. EBITDAX in that quarter was $249 million, and we generated $190 million of cash flow during the quarter. We reported adjusted net income of $28 million for Q3, or $0.09 per diluted share compared to a loss in the same period in 2024. Slide six is the year-to-date results. Our production for the first nine months have averaged 1.24 Bcfe per day.
With improved natural gas prices, our oil and gas sales in the first nine months have increased 18% to $1.1 billion. EBITDAX for the first nine months of 2025 was $802 million, and we generated $639 million of cash flow. We reported net income of $122 million for the first nine months of 2025, or $0.41 per diluted share as compared to a net loss for the same period last year. On slide seven, we break down our natural gas price realizations. The quarterly NYMEX settlement gas price averaged $3.07 in Q3, and the average Henry Hub spot price averaged $3.03, which is slightly below the settlement price.
28% of our gas was sold in the spot market and the balance was sold in the index market. The appropriate reference price for our gas was $3.06. Our realized gas price during the Q3 averaged $2.75, reflecting a $0.32 basis differential compared to the NYMEX settlement price, and a $0.31 differential compared to that reference price. In the Q3, we were 57% hedged, which increased our realized gas price to $2.99. We broke even from our third-party gas marketing in the Q3. On slide eight, we detail our operating costs per Mcfe and our EBITDAX margin. Our operating cost per Mcfe averaged $0.77 in the Q3, $0.03 lower than last quarter.
Our EBITDAX margin was 74% in Q3, which is unchanged from last quarter. Lifting costs improved by $0.02 in the quarter. Production ad valorem taxes were up by $0.01, and gathering and cash D&A costs improved by $0.01 in Q3. On slide nine, we recap our spending on drilling and other development activity. We spent a total of $267 million on development activities in Q3 and $785 million for the first nine months of this year. In the first nine months of this year, we've drilled 25 or 21.8 net horizontal Haynesville wells and 11 or 10 net Bossier wells for a total of 36 wells.
We also turned 36 wells or 30.9 net operated wells to sales, which had an average initial production rate of 27,000,000 cubic feet per day. Slide 10 recaps our capitalization at the end of Q3. We ended the quarter with $580 million of borrowings outstanding under our credit facility. Our borrowing base is at $2 billion under the credit facility, and the elected commitment is $1.5 billion. Our last 12 months leverage ratio has improved to 3x and will continue to improve as we get away from the 2024 results, which are weighed down by low natural gas prices. At the end of Q3, we had $239 million of liquidity. The sale of our Shelby Trough assets that's expected to close in December will improve the leverage ratio and enhance our liquidity, since the cash flow that's associated with the properties being sold was minimal. I'll now turn it over to Dan to discuss the drilling results.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Okay, thanks, Roland. If you look on slide 11, this is an overview of our latest acreage footprint in the Haynesville, Bossier Shale in East Texas and North Louisiana. We now have 1,055,386 gross and 797,440 net acres that are prospective for the commercial development of the Haynesville and Bossier Shales. Over on the left, this is our Western Haynesville acres footprint, which we've now grown to over 530,000 net acres. On the right is our 266,711 net acres in our Legacy Haynesville area. We have 27 gross or 26.9 net wells currently producing on our Western Haynesville acreage, which is virtually undeveloped compared to our Legacy Haynesville area.
Given the higher pay thickness and the higher pressures we encounter in the Western Haynesville, we expect the Western Haynesville will yield significantly more resource potential per section than our Legacy Haynesville. On slide 12, this outlines our new development plan utilizing the horseshoe lateral concept. The horseshoe well design concept combines the two separate and adjacent shorter laterals into a longer single lateral, which results in a much more efficient use of capital. We realize approximately 35% savings in our drilling costs when we drill a 10K lateral horseshoe well compared to a 5,000-foot sectional lateral well. Our drilling inventory in our Legacy Haynesville area now includes 118 horseshoe locations. During Q3, we completed our second horseshoe well to date.
The Roberts 26-23 #1 had 11,453 foot lateral and a 26,000,000 cubic feet per day IP rate. To date this year, we have drilled one additional horseshoe well, and we have another four horseshoe wells that are currently in progress. We plan to drill a total of eight horseshoe wells this year, and we plan to drill 10 horseshoe wells in 2026. Slide 13 is our updated drilling inventory in our Legacy Haynesville area at the end of Q3. This is adjusted to exclude the locations we're selling in the Shelby Trough. This quarter, we're now presenting our Legacy Haynesville and our Western Haynesville drilling locations separately.
Our total operated inventory in the Legacy Haynesville consists of 1,039 gross locations, 809 net locations, which equates to a working interest of approximately 78%. Our non-operated inventory in the Legacy Haynesville includes 873 gross locations, 108 net locations. This represents a 12% average of working interest. Our drilling inventory is comprised of short laterals, less than 5,000, medium laterals, between 5,000 and 8,500 feet, our long laterals between 8,500 and 10,000 feet, and our extra long laterals for all the wells over 10,000 feet. In our gross operated inventory in the Legacy Haynesville, we have 36 short laterals, 157 medium laterals, 425 long laterals, and 421 extra long laterals.
Our gross operated inventory is split, 51 in the Haynesville and 49% in the Bossier. Over 80% of our gross operated inventory in the Legacy Haynesville consists of laterals, which are greater than 8,500 feet. The 118 horseshoe locations mentioned on the previous slide are all in our legacy area. The average lateral length on inventory is now up to 9,961 feet. This is up 275 feet from the end of Q2. Our inventory provides us with decades of future drilling locations based on our current activity levels. On slide 14, we show our estimated drilling inventory in the Western Haynesville. This represents the first time where we've disclosed our Western Haynesville inventory.
Our total inventory in the Western Haynesville consists of 3,332 gross locations and 2,559 net locations. This equates to a working interest of about 77%. As much as our Western Haynesville acreage is not unitized, the net locations here are estimated. In the Western Haynesville, the inventory is more weighted to the Bossier formation, with 36% of the inventory in the Haynesville and 64% of the inventory in the Bossier. The same as our Legacy Haynesville inventory, our Western Haynesville inventory is broken down into groups of short laterals less than 5,000 ft, our medium laterals between 5,000 and 8,500 ft, our long laterals between 8,500 and 10,000 ft, and our extra long laterals over 10,000 ft.
In our Western Haynesville, in the gross operated inventory, we assume we have no short laterals. We have 1,347 medium laterals, 642 long laterals, and 1,343 extra long laterals. Approximately 60% of this gross operated inventory in the Western Haynesville consists of the laterals greater than 8,500 feet. On slide 15 is a chart outlining our average lateral lengths that we've drilled. This is based on wells that have reached total depth. The average lateral lengths are shown separately for both our Legacy Haynesville and Western Haynesville areas. In Q3, we drilled 11 wells to total depth in the Legacy Haynesville, and these had an average lateral length of 12,593 feet.
The individual lengths ranged from 4,968 feet up to 15,466 feet. Our record long lateral in our Legacy Haynesville area still stands at 17,409 feet. In Q3, we drilled six wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville. These wells had an average lateral length of 10,158 feet. The individual lengths here range from 7,809 feet up to 12,710 feet. Our longest lateral drilled to date in the Western Haynesville still stands at 12,763 feet. To date in the Western Haynesville, we have drilled 15 wells with laterals longer than 10,000 feet, and we have drilled six wells with laterals over 12,000 feet.
Slide 16 outlines the wells that were turned to sales on our Legacy Haynesville acreage this year. So far this year, we've turned 28 wells to sales in our Legacy Haynesville area. The individual IP rates on these wells range from 16,000,000 a day up to 37,000,000 cubic feet a day, and the average was 25,000,000 cubic feet a day. The average lateral length was 11,919 feet. With the individual wells ranging from 9,252 feet up to 17,409 feet. Just to recap, four of our eight rigs are drilling on our Legacy Haynesville acreage. Slide 17 outlines the eight wells that we have turned to sales in the Western Haynesville this year. Since we last reported our earnings, we have turned three additional wells to sales.
These three wells had an average lateral length of 8,566 feet and an average initial production rate of 32,000,000 cubic feet per day. Four of our eight rigs are drilling on our Western Haynesville acreage. Slide 18 highlights the average drilling days and the average footage drilled per day in the Legacy Haynesville area for our bench mark long lateral wells. These are our wells that are greater than 8,500 feet long. In Q3, we drilled 10 bench mark long lateral wells to total depth in the Legacy Haynesville. These wells averaged 26 days to total depth. We've averaged 26 days consistently for the last three quarters. In Q3, we averaged 1,004 feet drilled per day on our Legacy Haynesville acreage.
This is a 4.5% increase versus the Q2 2025, and a 2% increase versus the 2024 full year average of 987 feet drilled per day. The best well drilled to date in the Legacy Haynesville still stands at 1,461 feet, which was drilled to TD in 14 days. Slide 19 just highlights our drilling progress in the Western Haynesville. During the Q3, we drilled 6 wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville. We now have a total of 35 wells that we have drilled to total depth through the end of the quarter. We averaged 52 drilling days for the six wells drilled to total depth in the Q3.
This represents a decrease of three days compared to Q2, and a decrease of seven days compared to our 2024 full year average of 59 days. Our fastest oil drill to date, still stands at the 37-day mark, and that was drilled with a 12,045 foot lateral. Over on slide 20 is a summary of our D&C cost through Q3 for our benchmark long lateral wells located on our Legacy Haynesville acreage. These costs reflect all our legacy area wells drilled with laterals greater than 8,500 feet long. The drilling costs are based on when the wells reach TD, and the completion costs are based on when the wells are turned to sales. During Q3, we drilled 10 of our benchmark long lateral wells to total depth.
The Q3 drilling cost averaged $558 a foot. This is a 15% decrease compared to Q2. We had an abnormally high drilling cost in Q2 due to drilling difficulties that were associated with some highly overpressured SWD zones. During Q3, we turned nine wells to sales on our Legacy Haynesville acreage. The Q3 completion cost came in at $671 a foot. This represents a 7% decrease compared to Q2. These lower completion costs are due to a combination of, we had lower frack pricing, lower fuel costs with all of our wells using a natural gas blended fuel, and also the longer laterals in Q3.
We got four rigs running that are running on our Legacy Haynesville acreage. Slide 21 is a summary of the D&C costs through the end of Q3 for the wells drilled in the Western Haynesville. During the quarter, we drilled six wells to total depth, with an average lateral length of 10,158 feet. The Q3 drilling cost averaged $1,385 a foot. This represents a 24% decrease compared to Q2, but is more in line with our previous quarters. The primary factor for the lower drilling costs in Q3 is the longer laterals.
Our average lateral length in Q2 was very low at 7,933 feet, compared to an average lateral length of 10,158 feet in Q3. During the quarter, we also turned three wells to sales on our Western Haynesville acreage. These had an average lateral length of 8,566 feet. We didn't turn any wells to sales in Q1. The Q3 completion cost averaged $1,622 a foot. This is a 24% increase compared to Q2.
The higher completion cost was primarily due to the higher frack cost we had on the wells, to a lesser extent, the shorter average lateral length. We did have some higher than normal horsepower usage associated with frack in these wells, which were considerably deeper than our average Western Haynesville well, and we observed some higher frack gradients at these deeper depths. To kind of recap our activity levels. We've got four rigs running in the Western Haynesville, and we've got four rigs running on our Legacy Haynesville acreage. We also have two full-time dedicated frac fleets that we're running between both our Legacy Haynesville area and our Western Haynesville areas. I'll now turn the call back over to Jay.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
All right. Great job, Dan and Roland. Please refer to slide 22, where we summarize our outlook for 2025. In 2025, we remain primarily focused on building our great asset in Western Haynesville that will position us to benefit from the longer-term growth in natural gas demand. You know, we currently have four operated rigs drilling in Western Haynesville to continue to delineate the new play. We expect to drill 19 wells and turn 13 wells to sales in the Western Haynesville this year. We'll continue to build out our Western Haynesville midstream assets to keep up with the growing production from the area. Our new Marquez gas treating plant started operations in July, which more than doubled our gas treating capacity. In the Legacy Haynesville, we're currently running four rigs to build production back up in 2026.
We expect to drill 33 or 25.6 net wells and turn 35 or 28.2 net wells to sales in the Legacy Haynesville this year. We continue to have the industry's lowest producing cost structure and expect drilling efficiencies to continue to work toward driving down drilling and completion costs in 2025 in both the Western and Legacy Haynesville areas. You know, as Roland stated earlier, we have strong financial liquidity totaling more than $900 million, which will be enhanced with proceeds from the Shelby Trough divestiture, which is expected to close December 2025. If you have any specific questions on guidance for the rest of the year, please feel free to reach out to Ron Mills. Ron?
Ron Mills
VP of Finance and Investor Relations, Comstock Resources
Antoine, we can turn it over to Q&A.
Operator
Thank you. At this time, we will conduct the question and answer session. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please stand by while I compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from Derrick Whitfield from Texas Capital. Please go ahead.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director, Texas Capital
Good morning, all, and thanks for your time.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director, Texas Capital
Wanted to start with a broader question around 2026, and not to pin you guys down on any numbers. Really just want to think about it from the standpoint of the higher level of activity you're carrying into 2026 and the operational efficiencies you've gained in both the Western Haynesville and Legacy Haynesville. Could you speak to the broader capital efficiency gains you'd expect as you enter the year?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I'd say, you know, we've. They're kind of two different animals, the Legacy Haynesville versus the Western Haynesville. I mean, the efficiency gains in the, you know, the legacy area, we pretty much, you know, we're kind of up at the top of the curve there. I think we've picked up a lot, obviously, since we've added the Horseshoe wells. You know, as far as just being able to convert a lot of our shorter wells to longer wells, I think we've seen more efficiency there. The Horseshoe wells are going great for us. Really the efficiency gains that we're still looking to pick up and have been, you know, still up on the learning curve is in the Western Haynesville. You know, we've had a lot of improvements we've made to date.
We still got a few other things kind of, you know, coming down the pike that we're gonna be looking at implementing in the Western Haynesville to help our efficiencies there. You know, I think the four rigs that we got running in the Western Haynesville's is a good activity level for us. You know, we're able to learn a lot from it. We've got, we've made a lot of improvements in our downhole performance. You know, like I said, we just got a few things in the mill that are kinda churning that are gonna help us out, we think, in this next year in 2026.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, Derrick, you commented that we've had solid Western Haynesville well results, I'd just like to comment on Dan. The very first Haynesville well we ever drilled back in 2008, Dan was involved with it. For 17 years, he's touched every Bossier or Haynesville well we've drilled, either it be in the core or in the Western Haynesville. You know, he has complete authority to de-risk and optimize the cost on the new Western Haynesville play. That's important.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Just from a capital efficiency standpoint, you know, we are carrying some capital this year for the addition of that eighth rig with no production really showing up until sometime in Q1 or Q2 of next year. When you think about your typical capital efficiency, that should drive improved capital efficiency next year.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director, Texas Capital
Great. For my follow-up, I wanted to shift over to gas marking. More specifically, I love your perspective on how you see gas and gas competition unfolding along the Gulf Coast. As you think about your supply advantage of being able to deliver gas into Sabine Pass and the competing demand opportunities between LNG and power gen, you're arguably in a great position to benefit from both in terms of gas realization.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's a good observation, Derrick. Yeah. I think that especially owning our own midstream in the Western Haynesville is gonna be a really huge asset for us in the future as we're able to kind of, instead of having to go through other midstream companies and long-haul pipelines, you know, we can create great markets, you know, right there, that we can directly sell to end users and become a very reliable supplier. I think that's what a lot of these, you know, large users with new demand are looking to establish direct relationships with the producers, and you've heard a lot about that in our industry. I think we're well-positioned there, given that we control the infrastructure of the midstream.
Obviously, a great location where, you know, yeah, the gas can support all the growth in Texas. Then, you know, with the Port Arthur LNG, you know, very close to being able to connect to that. I think that's a big part of the future of... for natural gas, is just not only having the natural gas, but being able to, you know, get it directly to the end user.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, Derrick, I think it's, you know, if you look at location, location, I mean, 100 mi from Dallas and the same distance from Houston, and really close to LNG corridor, you're perfectly situated for both AI data centers and LNG. You couldn't be in a better area. The fact that, you know, this is not an exploration play, it's really a development play for the geology that was there. It's been a very active oil and gas region for 30+ years.
For us to just deepen these wells with the new technology, in a great footprint where we're located, you know, and on maybe 6,000 of these acres are dedicated, the rest are undedicated. That's why we say, you know, we were around a big, you know, bright light bulb, and then people are calling because of the inventory, which inventory is the Holy Grail. I mean, that's why you see people expanding to look at this play. It is the Holy Grail. You gotta have inventory.
Derrick Whitfield
Managing Director, Texas Capital
Thanks for your comments. I'll turn it back to the operator.
Operator
Thank you. One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Charles Meade from Johnson Rice. Please go ahead.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Good morning, Jay, to you and your whole team there.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Hello, Charles.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Thank you for the warm welcome. Jay, I wanna ask you about the Shelby Trough sale. That looks to us like that's a really great outcome for you guys as far as, you know, what the seller paid for those undeveloped locations. I wanted to see how you would characterize it, how happy you were with those proceeds, and ask if there's anything left in your portfolio that would, you know, that could fit that same appetite for people who are willing to, you know, pay for those undeveloped locations.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, first of all, Charles, I think it's a total win-win for everybody. I mean, we're really a unicorn out there because we have so much inventory. You know, as we just announced, we almost had 2,600 locations net in the Western Haynesville. That's a big gift that we've been working on for five years. If you look at other really good locations that might be for sale, I mean, I think it was a really smart buy by the buyer. I think we needed to pay down the debt on our balance sheet because we'd incurred a lot of money as our investment in the Western Haynesville. We looked at that. You know, we trimmed some of the vertical wells.
Those 900 or so vertical wells, those, we sold those early on. We are always looking as we de-risk, and kind of fortify our acreage position, Western Haynesville. Is there anything else we can do? That is to adjust the balance sheet because we need to get our leverage lower. I was pleased with how both of those transactions came about. Again, we always look to see, Charles, as you well know, what can we do as a company positioned where we think we are, to become a stronger company in the light of, you know, AI, data center demand, and LNG demand. That's the only thing we do. You know, I think everybody won in the trade. Great locations, and that we didn't need to be drilling them because we're drilling the Western Haynesville.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Got it. Then, I, you know, following on that same thread, I want to say thank you for sharing this Western Haynesville location count. I just want to ask a couple of questions around, you know, your assumptions and the dynamics there. Just using the kind of back of the envelope math, it looks like you guys have been pretty conservative in your assumptions on number of zones and spacing across zones. I wonder if you could share if you'd be willing to share what the important assumptions are in that, you know, I think the 2,500, 2,600 number.
I think Dan alluded to this in his, in his, prepared remarks that perhaps the, perhaps because not a lot of the acreage is unitized yet, that's actually preventing you from counting location and, you know, my assumption is that would get worked out over time, but maybe you can fold that into the assumptions on the location count.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
I'm sure. I think we tried to be conservative on how we looked at, you know, well spacing and benches in the play, you know, 'cause you obviously don't wanna start out at a high number and bring it down. We think they're very... You know, it's a very realistic view of the inventory. The, the comment that was made about the working interest, the tip in our Legacy Haynesville inventory, I mean, every single location there is pretty exact. We know the exact... We know what unit it's in. We know our working interest with precision. In the Western Haynesville, those units are being put together still, so, you know, the exact working interest in the units, is not, you know, 100% known. You know, so far, most of the wells, you know, we've had 100% working in-interest in.We, you know, just looked at our acreage ownership and just made some rougher assumptions there. It just doesn't have the level of precision, but I don't think it's a significant, you know. I think we're within the margin of error as far as looking at, you know, how we present the net numbers.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, Charles, you always discount it back. You know, you say, here's what you could have. Here's kind of a high-low number, and then you discount it back and say, okay, what is a number that we can throw out right now that we think, you know, with some bookends on, we have a chance of achieving? Like Alden said, you don't wanna be aggressive, and then all of a sudden you have a few less and you know, you're a loser. We wanna throw that out and just say, again, with an asterisk that, you know, we've not unitized some of those locations, so it's a guesstimate.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Got it. That is great detail. Thank you.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, great questions.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Kalei Akamine from Bank of America. Please go ahead.
Kalei Akamine
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
Hey, good morning, guys. Jay, Roland.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Kalei Akamine
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
I wanna start on the Western Haynesville disclosure. Maybe first off, I think putting your expectations in print really shows your conviction in the asset. For my question, I wanna follow up on the unitization comment. You've got some short laterals in that table, 5,000 to 8,500 feet. This is a large contiguous position. My question is, what's stopping you from doing the land work to optimize the entire position around 10,000 foot laterals? If that's possible, how long would that work take?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's a, that's a great question, too. I think there are some areas that where there's the ownership, where there's, you know, some other operators that, you know, that we've already identified that we're, you know, we're keeping out of our units. We've chosen those shorter laterals. Just like, you know, the wells we completed, you know, this quarter and drilled last quarter, a lot of that was defined by, you know, kind of the acreage ownership. We've honored that, you know, where we don't have it completely contiguous. I think there's obviously geologic structures that we have identified on seismic that we, you know, are avoiding and not wanting to develop, you know, and around.
You know, we've honored a lot of our geologic work, too, in those assumptions. It's still, you know, early on, you'll be able to probably optimize that over time. A lot will depend on how long do you really wanna go. Do you wanna go to, you know, 15,000 foot laterals? Some of that is I think there's room to optimize in the future, but I think this was a really good view of how we see the acreage we currently own. Now, we could also lease additional acreage that will change the configuration in the future, and I'm sure that will happen. We're always picking up additional acreage as we put units together. There will be moving parts, but I do feel like this was a pretty thorough look at, if we stop leasing, you know, what it could look like now.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, Kalei, you notice we added, you know, 5,000 acres from the last time we reported. We do clean up stuff all the time, in the Western Haynesville, just like we do in the core. This is a pretty, you know, safe, conservative number. We think that we have leased 90% of what we think the real value is in the Western Haynesville. Maybe that's expanded, and it'll be a good thing. We hope it does expand. Based upon the control that we have and the sizes we have and the well results we have, you know, I think that we're in pretty good shape there. We keep trying to make it better. At some point in time, we won't own 100% of all the wells. Until that time is right, you know, we'll kinda drill the lateral lengths that we need to keep the information that we need to keep kind of in our back pocket right now.
Kalei Akamine
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
Thank you for that, guys. For my second question, I wanna ask about the second train at the Marquez Gas Plant. That build looks like it's gonna take you to about 1.3 Bcf from 900,000,000 cubic feet, so that's quite the scale. My question is, was this part of the original scope of the JV deal with Quantum? Can you talk about the capacity utilization at those plants? What is it today? Once Marquez 2 is online, perhaps in 2027, where do you think the utilization rate will be at that time?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
I don't know if we wanna forecast the utilization rate. That's getting way out there. You know, we are, you know. When we originally put together the plan for Pinnacle, the Pinnacle Gas Services and how to service the development program, I mean, obviously we saw, and we've commented this a long time ago, that we saw trying to create a treating infrastructure to handle up to 2 Bcf of gross production, you know, over the next five, six, seven years.
I think this is the second phase of Marquez is just was the next step that was in our original plan. There's, you know, another, you know, either debating on either a expansion at Bethel or a third gas plant will probably be something way off, you know, next in the future. We do have to keep ahead. You know, we obviously have to provide for the treating way ahead of when we're gonna actually produce it. It's not gonna be a just-in-time kind of delivery, obviously, because it takes a good 12 to 18 months to put those together. Yeah, right now on Marquez phase II, we've got a lot of long lead time of...
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Equipment
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Components and equipment that are being manufactured that, you know. We have to go out and order. That's kind of the big process going on now, you know, for something that we can hopefully open up next summer, would be our goal for that.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yes, I think the key answer to that is, we have a lot of inventory, but we own our midstream, as Roland mentioned at the beginning comments. You know, we have an incredible financial partner with Quantum, and we look to see what our drilling inventory looks like. We see what our performance looks like. We see what our acreage addition looks like. Then based upon all that, we control the gathering. As far as the takeaway and the demand, as we said, you know, 45 minutes ago, it has never, ever looked brighter out there for what the world needs, not just America, the world needs in the form of natural gas. I think we're right there at the right time.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. With their addition, you have other operators. There are a couple of other operators with which are running rigs in the area, you know. You know, how we actually build out will also depend on do we end up picking up some of that gas or not. That's all, you know, a lot of that is to kind of remain to be seen in the future. There's other activity in the area that hopefully that we kind of see coming to Pinnacle over time too, as we build out, you know, that great asset that underlies the Western Haynesville.
Kalei Akamine
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
Guys, I appreciate all that color. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Carlos Escalante from Wolfe Research. Please go ahead.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Thank you. I love the way the operator said my name, Escalante. Good morning, Jay, Roland, and Dan. I want to go back to one of your comments, Jay. You said, you know, hopefully, the Western Haynesville, the footprint that you guys have at least expands, and, you know, nice wordplay, by the way. Look, you've done a great job at establishing the core with just under 30 tails across the place, especially in that southern corridor across Leon and Robertson, with its incremental data proving up acreage to the north of that as well. However, you've seen recent leasing and M&A activity load into the east and southeast, particularly in Anderson and Houston.
I wonder, when you see that, do you think the core... Do you think there's likelihood that the core of the basin could actually be much larger, and it extends into, potentially some of your other wells that you tilled earlier this year? In part beats the question, if I may, along the same lines, if you look at... It looks like you have a permitted well near Olajuwon. If maybe you can touch on when you plan to go back to this area as well. Thank you.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, yeah. The comment would be because of Jerry Jones and because of his, you know, big and plus dollar investment in the company, we could literally think, and not only think, Carlos, we could act out of the box. Because of the fact that we've always been leaning toward natural gas, I mean, and we're one of the front runners in the core of the Legacy Haynesville area. Jerry Jones said, you know, here's a well. We've showed it. We could drill it, and that's a Circle M well. That over the last five years has proved to be successful.
As we move to the call we have today over five years, in looking at the seismic 2D, 3D, looking at the well bore penetrations, looking at the performance of the 30, 40 wells we've either drilled, completed or drilling, what we look at, we say, we're very comfortable that, you know, this is probably 90% of the real value. Now, you know, as you look at Aethon says there are monster wells out there. I love that they say that, we've hit a bunch of them. You know, that's a credible company. Mitsui to come in, they're smart. Management's smart. Their money's smart. You know, they come in. You know, Expand is, they're doing what their name says, expanding. Their name says expanding, they're expanding into the Western Haynesville.
Because why? As I said earlier, the locations are the holy grail. I mean, you can do M&A, M&A, M&A, but that doesn't add any new locations on planet Earth. It gives you more under your umbrella. We've tried to, you know, to address the problem, and the problem is, can you really add new inventory? That's where, you know, the prior question was asked, what's your inventory count? I think we're pretty accurate on, you know, 2,500, 2,600 net locations. That's an incredible number. You know, 2,600 locations, incredible number. We are always looking, Carlos, to say, Do you go east? Do you go south? Do you go... Everybody is always doing that. You know what? There's gonna be some gems out there, and I hope that... I hope they are found, because all that does is make our acreage more valuable, in our opinion.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
I'll add [crosstalk].
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Appreciate. Oh.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
You asked about a permitted well up by the Olajuwon 1. We actually did spud. We got a two-well pad that's up there near the Olajuwon 1. That pad was spudded last week.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
It'll be one Bossier, one Haynesville?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, we got one. The Ellijay one is producing from the Haynesville, and the new pad that we spudded last week will be a additional Haynesville well and a Bossier test, our first Bossier test up there.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, and, you know, we're coring up in that area too.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
That's correct.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
That's important that at the cores we've had, and we're, you know, we're coring there also.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
That's terrific, colleague, guys. I appreciate that. Real quick, if I can sneak in my follow-up. You mentioned Aethon, Jay. If I may, I think one of your tilled wells this quarter, two wells, the McCullough wells, are nearby that area. We've seen their type curves to be quite outstanding in terms of production plateau. Obviously, this well is very strong in terms of initial production. I guess my question is there anything that you're looking at in terms of what they're doing or any kind of near-term collaboration that you can, guys, potentially benefit from in terms of what you do? Has it been more a separate effort from that standpoint?
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, you know, we've done some, are in the process of doing some acreage swaps with them, so they can drill longer laterals. We can drill some longer laterals in areas that we wanna drill and they wanna drill. I don't have any other comments on that, Dan, on McCullough et cetera, versus Aethon. I mean...
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
It's always very, when you have other operators doing things differently, it's always great learning for a basin. That's one thing that the Western Haynesville hasn't had near as much of as the original Haynesville had. You know, as we have some new other operators and they were the first one out there. It's gonna be, I think very incremental to, you know, us learning how to properly produce the wells and drill the wells. The more activity, the more learning, it's gonna be better for all the operators.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
If you have four or five more new operators come in, I think everybody, particularly Comstock, the learning curve is shortened. It, I think, be a great thing.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I think what you see is all the operators, obviously, they all kinda do something a little bit different. Bigger fracs, smaller fracs, you know, how they draw their wells down, you know, what kind of casing design, you know, bigger hole laterals, slimmer hole laterals. All of those things, I think when you get more of that in the pot and start looking at the results, you know, like we say, that's definitely gonna help everybody.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Thank you, fellas. Thank you for having me on.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thanks, Carlos.
Operator
Thank you. To ask a question, please press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. In the interest of time, we ask that you please ask one question and one follow-up. Our next question comes from Kevin MacCurdy from Pickering Energy Partners. Please go ahead.
Kevin MacCurdy
Managing Director, Pickering Energy Partners
Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking my questions. I know you haven't put out a 2026 guide yet. Is there any color you can provide on how you plan to prosecute the Western Haynesville next year? I'm looking for any thoughts on holding acreage versus development, the size of the pads you might drill and lateral lengths as well. I think you kinda touched on where you might be drilling. Any more color on that would be helpful too.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
I think that, you know, the 90% of the plan is gonna be holding acreage, as we said. You know, we still have a lot of term acreage that we leased in the play. That's a big part of where we wanna drill the wells. It's gonna be following, you know, where we leased, the timeframe we leased. I think that's how we look at it. I think, yeah, the activity level of four rigs that we have operating, you know, is sufficient to kind of accomplish all that and not have to, you know, worry about losing any acreage that we don't drill, that we wanna drill.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
I think you're gonna see in 2026, more of our wells will, you know, will continue to kinda push more in that, you know, northerly, northeastern direction along the trend of where the acreage is.
Kevin MacCurdy
Managing Director, Pickering Energy Partners
Great. Appreciate that detail. Then just a question on slide 13 and 14 on your inventory. Just to confirm, were the changes in the Legacy Haynesville and Bossier Shale, was that just driven by the asset sales, or was there anything else that changed in those inventory numbers?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, one time we had some of the Western Haynesville in there, probably a small amount, that was based on just the wells we drilled and, you know, the direct offsets, et cetera, that you obviously have in the inventory. That's why we kinda chose to break it out. It really wasn't really represented much in the original chart. You had that, plus you had, you know, obviously, we had the acreage that we sold or in the process of selling, that we also removed those locations. Then there's always continued recalibration.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
As, you know, as wells or as we find a way to make the laterals longer. You could see that the feed continues to get larger, you know, average foot of that lateral. That's always a process that we continue to optimize.
Kevin MacCurdy
Managing Director, Pickering Energy Partners
Thank you for taking my question.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Jacob Roberts from TPH & Co. Please go ahead.
Jacob Roberts
Director of Research, TPH&Co
Good morning.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Jacob Roberts
Director of Research, TPH&Co
I wanted to circle back to a Q2 item. One of the things that was discussed was some experimentation on choke management in the Western Haynesville. I understand that we probably don't have enough data to make a final call, but I'm just wondering if you could talk about maybe the varying methodologies you've applied to the three that came online last quarter, and then the handful that are gonna be coming online to end the year.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. We got the three that we turned to sales in Q3. We've got four new wells that are turning to sales here in Q4. We have had some. We have varied it a little bit. I'd say we haven't done anything that's been extremely conservative to date. You know, we're taking some of the information from the cores, and we're still, you know, doing a lot of detailed rate transient analysis. You know, basically, I think it's telling us, obviously, the more conservative drawdown is what we need to be following. I think, you know, for the future, we're still looking to transition, you know, more into that, probably more conservative approach from where we started at.
Jacob Roberts
Director of Research, TPH&Co
Great. Thank you. Jay, earlier you mentioned AI data centers, that type of stuff, as well as LNG demand, which have both been hugely topical. Recently, we saw one of your peers sign a sizable industrial contract at a premium to NYMEX over in Louisiana. Curious if you could talk about that market, how you see it evolving and maybe Comstock's willingness to participate in industrial agreements moving forward.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Sure. That's a great market, especially in the along the river corridor area and areas along the Gulf Coast where there are new, you know, new industrial plastic plants, et cetera, that are being built, fertilizer plants. They're competing, obviously, with the LNG feedstock gas, you know. Those customers have been reaching out and interested in long-term supply deals where, you know, you know, years ago, they were never interested in that. They would just go get gas, you know. In the monthly market, it was easy to get.
I think over time, we see a lot of our market and other producers in the area, you know, wanting to establish, you know, having more direct sales to end users, capturing more of the value chain and, you know, better margins versus, you know, having the midstream companies, you know, take off a lot of that margin. You know, a lot of us are working on long-term plans like that as we are too.
Jacob Roberts
Director of Research, TPH&Co
Great. Appreciate the time, guys.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Phillips Johnston from Capital One. Please go ahead.
Phillips Johnston
Senior E&P Analyst, Capital One
Phillip, thanks for the time, and congrats on the asset sales. My first question is really just a housekeeping question for Roland on the Shelby Trough sale. Would you expect any tax leakage on the gross proceeds?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. That's a good question. No, we really have lots of tax attributes to actually that. Yeah, we do expect a fairly sizable gain on that transaction because of, you know, we acquired that acreage way back at the Covey Park acquisition, and it wasn't a big part of that value that got allocated then. You know, there is a pretty sizable book and tax gain that we expect. You'll see, kind of see some of that in the 10-Q when we file it later today. We think we have a lot of tax attributes that we'll just be able to utilize, we don't see any cash, you know, real cash tax impact of that.
Phillips Johnston
Senior E&P Analyst, Capital One
Okay. Sounds good. A question for Dan, and it's really a follow-up on Carlos and Kevin's questions. It sounds like the two well pad near Olajuwon is kicked off, which is good to hear. Can you maybe just give us a guesstimate of how many wells up in that northern step out area might be considered for next year? Or what percentage of the total might be up in that area?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Good question. We do have more wells planned for up in the area up there. I've the number off, you know, escapes me off the top of my head. We do really like that area up there. The Olajuwon is performing extremely well. Super happy with it. Our next step, you know, is on this two-well pad is to test the Bossier, which is much thicker up there. We wanna get a good read on the Bossier, and then, you know, we'll kinda go from there as far as how we're gonna develop out that bench in that area. We do have, I'm gonna say, you know, five, six wells kinda planned up in that area for next year, kind of around, you know, just around that general area.
Phillips Johnston
Senior E&P Analyst, Capital One
Yep. Okay. Perfect. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Noel Parks from Tuohy Brothers Investment Research. Please go ahead.
Noel Parks
Managing Director, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Hi. Good morning.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Noel Parks
Managing Director, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
I just had a couple. Hey, how you doing? You know, you did touch a bit on it, but with the new treatment capacity you have, the new plant coming online, have you talked much about sort of like the economics of it, sort of the in-house economics versus the third-party opportunity, you know, while you're kind of in the? The ramp up mode.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I think that's been something we've been, you know, studying, obviously, you know, 'cause we don't, you know. A large part of, of your cost for treating is really all the facilities you build. Once you build them, if you can utilize them, you know, your actual operating costs can be very, very, you know, very, very low, just the actual operating cost associated with it. You have to recover the capital, that's kind of where a lot of the costs are. Obviously, if you own it yourself, once you recover it, you don't have to keep recovering it.
If you allow a third party to provide it, then they're gonna continue to charge whatever they can for that area based on, you know, demand for their services in the area. That cost will never go down unless, you know, there's just no demand for services in the area. I think these are long-term investments we're making now, but I think they're really gonna really pay off, you know, in the future, you know, for us and to continue to preserve our, you know, already industry-leading low-cost structure. That's why, you know, we're real excited about what we're able to accomplish out there and be able to do it, you know, without too big of a strain on the company with our partnership there that's funding it.
Noel Parks
Managing Director, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Great. Thanks. This is kind of a housekeeping item, but I did take sort of a quick look at the gathering and transportation expense line, and it looked like it might have been down sequentially a bit in the quarter. I just wonder if I had that right and if there were any drivers behind that?
Ron Mills
VP of Finance and Investor Relations, Comstock Resources
Yeah, it was down sequentially. It was just over $41 million in Q2. It was just under $40 million in Q3. Part of that is driven by we had lower volume sequentially as well. You look at it on a GTC per unit basis, it was $0.36 just versus $0.37 last quarter. That's driven by volumes.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I would say that's probably correct. You're right.
Noel Parks
Managing Director, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Okay. Okay, great. Thanks a lot.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Paul Diamond from Citi. Please go ahead.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Morning all. Thanks for taking the call. Just wanted to touch quickly on kind of your activity allocation between Western Haynesville and Legacy acreage, kind of split 50/50. If you guys were to add or to drop any activity over time, where do you think it would come from, one or the other?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, you know, I think we'd like to keep the four operating rigs in the Western Haynesville because, just because of the strategically, you know, in order to hold all the acreage, that makes that a comfortable program. I think, yeah, we'd obviously reflect in the Legacy area where there's no acreage considerations there, and you're kind of basing that on, you know, what's the supply demand outlook? What's the price? The, you know, obviously, just like last year, we flexed very heavily in the Legacy area, and we hope to continue just to steadily add activity to Western Haynesville as we build that up. So they're the kinda, you know, two different kinda. I think we're very reactive on the Legacy side to, you know, the situation, and then we wanna be more, you know, steady on the Western Haynesville in order to continue to develop that asset and retain that asset.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Got it. Makes perfect sense. Now that you guys are giving the inventory assumptions at the Western Haynesville acreage, can you talk about any progression you see on D&C? Still tracking towards about $30 million per well on 10,000-foot basis. I guess, where do you guys see that going through time? What's your target longer term?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
I think we're gonna definitely see the cost continue to come down. You know, there's a pretty good spread depending on where you're drilling at on the acreage as far as, you know, what that D&C cost is. You know, our low, you know, our low end that we've achieved so far is about $2,100 a foot, you know, for the stuff that's a little bit shallower TVD. You know, the $30 million mark or assuming like a 10K lateral, $3,000 a foot or a little bit higher than that. You know, if you go all the way to the other end, to the far deeper stuff, you know, probably just a little bit over that.
You know, as far as any quarter when we're reporting, you know, it just depends on where those rigs have been and what, you know, what the TVD areas we're drilling in as far as what the cost comes out to. We're definitely gonna see the cost continue to go down. I think we've gotten, you know, a big chunk of it down already, and as, you know, naturally go on time, I think the rate at which the costs come down probably slow a little bit. We still see, you know, I mentioned it earlier, we still got a few things, you know, kinda coming down the pike that we're gonna be trying. We think that's gonna help us, you know, continue to shave days off.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. Makes perfect sense. I'll leave it there. Thanks.
Operator
Thank you. This concludes the question and answer session. I will now turn it back over to Jay Allison for closing remarks.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Perfect. I wanna thank everybody for listening for over an hour. You know, 4 November 2025 is a great day for the company when we can tell the stakeholders, which is you, and our financial backers, which is you, that, you know, we've added this giant footprint in the Western Haynesville. The debt that we have, that is the Western Haynesville acreage that we have been buying. You know, it's 530,000 net acres. But we can report on a day like today, we have over $900 million liquidity, and that's gonna grow.
We can report that we have, you know, 2,559 Western Haynesville locations at the very beginning of time, and then the legacy locations are 917. We have a lot of inventory. We're not chasing inventory, or we're not chasing M&A. The management here has been a pioneer as a Haynesville Bossier shale going back to 2008, 17 years. You know, the man that's in charge of operations has been here, the very first day we ever looked at the Haynesville Bossier, which is Dan Harrison.
You look at managing the balance sheet, the couple of divestitures that we will make and have made, that just shows you that we're watching our balance sheet, which, you know, the major stockholder and everybody else wants us to do that. I just wanna thank you for believing in the company, and we'll give you a good day's work every day. Thank you for the call.
Operator
Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.

Operator
Thank you for standing by, and welcome to Comstock Resources Q2 fiscal year 2022 earnings conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen only mode. After the speaker presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. I would now like to hand the call over to Jay Allison, Chairman and CEO. Please go ahead.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources Inc
All right. Thank you. You got a good tone this morning. You start everybody off right. Let me tell you, we're thankful to be a natural gas producer in the Haynesville, which we think is the best base in North America to have dry natural gas. Anyhow, welcome to the Comstock Resources Q2 2022 financial and operating results conference call. You can view a slide presentation during or after this call by going to our website at www.comstockresources.com and downloading the quarterly results presentation. There you'll find a presentation titled Q2 2022 Results. I'm Jay Allison, the Chief Executive Officer of Comstock. With me is Roland Burns, our President and Chief Financial Officer, Dan Harrison, our Chief Operating Officer, and Ron Mills, our VP of Finance and Investor Relations.
If you'll flip over to two, please refer to slide two in our presentation to note that our discussions today will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of securities laws. While we believe the expectations in such statements to be reasonable, there can be no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct. Now starts the real presentation. Slide three, the Q2 2022 highlights. We cover the highlights of Q2 on slide three. In Q2, we generated $190 million of operating free cash flow. We also retired $271 million of our senior notes, including the redemption of our 7.5 senior notes we assumed when we acquired Covey Park, and we repurchased $26 million of our 6.75 Senior notes in the open market.
We brought our leverage down to 1.2x. Our EBITDAX for the quarter came in at $515 million or 105% higher than last year. Our operating cash flow increased 133% to $458 million or $0.65/diluted share. Revenues after hedging for the quarter were $604 million and 86% higher than last year. Our adjusted net income for the quarter was $274 million or $1/diluted share. Our Haynesville drilling program is going well, as demonstrated by the 14 or 12.6 net operated wells that we reported on this quarter, with an average initial production rate of 26 million cubic feet per day.
We completed a very attractive bolt-on acquisition, which included approximately 60,000 net acres prospective for the Haynesville and Bossier Shale, and a 145-mile high pressure pipeline, and natural gas treating plant for $36 million. We also achieved certification for our natural gas production under the MiQ standard for methane emissions measurement, which demonstrates our environmental stewardship. I will now turn the call over to Roland Burns to comment on our financial results. Roland.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources Inc
All right. Thanks, Jay. On slide four, we recap the very strong financial results we had for Q2. Pro forma for the sale of our Bakken properties, which we completed last October, our production increased by 1% to 1.4 Bcfe/day. On a pro forma basis, our adjusted EBITDAX for the quarter grew by 122% over 2021's Q2 to $515 million, and it was driven mostly by stronger natural gas prices.
